newsitem.title: USA: AOL reaches pact on pricing with 19 states. [CORRECTED 23:36 GMT]
newsitem.headline: AOL reaches pact on pricing with 19 states. [CORRECTED 23:36 GMT]

text.p: America Online Inc. Thursday reached a settlement with the attorneys general of 19 states over its new flat-rate pricing plan, agreeing to pay automatic refunds to its subscribers who do not want to pay $19.95 a month.
(Corrects headline and throughout to make clear agreement reached with 19 states, not 20)
Last month, the world's largest online service announced a new pricing plan of unlimited access for $19.95 a month, vs. its previous plan of $9.95 a month for five hours.

On Dec. 1, AOL automatically switched all subscribers to the new plan, unless members notified AOL that they did not want it. Many states said the practice was deceptive, because the change was implemented "in a manner that was misleading."

The pact, announced by Massachusetts Attorney General Scott Harshbarger and filed in state court in Boston, calls on AOL to provide refunds to subscribers who ask to switch back to their old plan before March 31, 1997.
Attorneys general from 18 other states and Guam took part in the agreement.
"Today's agreement secures automatic funds for AOL members who do not want the company's more expensive flat-rate plan," Harshbarger said in a statement.

"The common sense principles of consumer protection do not end in cyberspace," Harshbarger said. "Companies should not be allowed to change the terms of an agreement with their customers in ways that make it difficult for them to understand or accept the new terms."
A spokesman for Dulles, Va.-based AOL praised the pact and said it would not have much effect on the company's financial results.

"We are happy to have reached the agreement and happy to be moving forward with the new unlimited pricing," the spokesman said. "We believe the unlimited pricing offers the best value on the Internet and the response has been overwhelming."
AOL said on Monday that it was spending $250 million to upgrade its network, to deal with the surge in demand that accompanied its move to flat-rate pricing.

According to the agreement with the states, AOL must obtain consent to billing changes from as many of its 7 million subscribers as possible. A "pop-up" screen will ask subscribers to agree to the new plan or pick another option.
AOL must also automatically provide retroactive refunds to all consumers who ask to switch back to their old plan before March 31, 1997.

AOL will provide a toll-free number to handle inquiries and complaints regarding the new flat-rate service and it must notify its members of their rights and obligations regarding the automatic conversion via U.S. mail and in a series of online screens.

The other states were Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Hawaii, Iowa, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Texas, Vermont, Wisconsin. The agreement also included the territory of Guam.
Last week, the state of Washington announced a similar agreement with America Online.
AOL stock fell 12.5 cents to $40 on the New York Stock Exchange.
